name: Verne Moon
lines: From the Earth to the Moon
Jules Verne · From the Earth to the Moon (1865), translated by Louis Mercier and Eleanor E. King, the whole book
the Gun Club's notice, on its front on the quay (21 Union Square, Baltimore)
Jules Verne · Round the Moon (1870), translated by Louis Mercier and Eleanor E. King, the whole book
the crane over the Columbiad's mouth, Stone's Hill
Gentlemen: the Moon.
My friend! What a voyage we shall have!
Figures, sir. Show me the figures.
Hurrah for the Gun Club!
Welcome to Cambridge. The Moon is very clear tonight.
Mind the trucks: the well is deep.
🌍 The Earth, enormous, filling the floor-scuttle: its night side towards you, a thin crescent of daylight at its rim.
✨ Black sky and stars without number, sharp, unwinking. The Earth a great crescent below; the Moon a little brighter, higher, ahead.
⚖️ The Earth and the Moon, nearly of a size: the neutral point, where neither pulls harder.
🌕 The Moon, close: mountains, craters, plains of grey, every shadow cut black.
🏔️ The Moon's northern lands, very close: crater after crater, the Sea of Cold, and the pole ahead.
🌑 Night. The Moon is a black hole cut in the stars. The cold comes through the walls.
☀️ Sunlight again, blinding: the southern mountains of the Moon, and Tycho, the brightest thing on her face.
🌖 The Moon going away from the scuttles, larger than the Earth, but smaller every hour.
🌍 The Earth, growing in the floor-scuttle, faster and faster: you are falling home.
💥 The Gun Club, 21 Union Square, Baltimore.
Its walls hung with every kind of gun; its chandeliers made of revolvers; its president's chair on a carved gun-carriage. Barbicane has a proposal: the Moon.
The President's chair
look at the President's chair

🪑 A chair on a carved gun-carriage, its back in red leather, a little bronze mortar for an inkstand on the table before it. From here Barbicane rules the Gun Club; it is said he has never once raised his voice.
THE GUN CLUB · SOUTH OF THE 28th PARALLEL
The map of Florida and Texas
🗺️ The 28th parallel ruled in red across the Gulf: south of it, the Moon passes straight overhead. Only two states of the Union reach below it: Texas and Florida.
SUBSCRIPTIONS · URBI ET ORBI
The subscription board
read the subscription board
💰 The whole world's subscriptions, chalked up country by country. One line is short: Great Britain, nothing at all.
The committee table
look at the committee's papers
📐 Drawings of a shell, round and then pointed; a gun drawn nine hundred feet long; and sheet after sheet of J. T. Maston's sums, covered with x and n.
The newspaper rack
read the newspapers
📰 The New York Herald: 'THE MOON! THE GUN CLUB'S GREAT PROJECT.'
📰 The Tampa Observer: 'FLORIDA, AND NOWHERE ELSE.'
📰 The Galveston Journal: 'TEXAS HAS TWENTY-SIX COUNTIES. FLORIDA HAS TWELVE.'
📰 The Philadelphia Ledger: a letter from Captain Nicholl, with five wagers in it.
A member of the Gun Club

of the Gun Club of Baltimore, in Jules Verne's From the Earth to the Moon (1865): an artillery officer of the late war, proud of your wounds and your guns, bored to death by the peace, eager for Barbicane's great project.
Peace! There's nothing left for a gunner to do.
Members are requested to attend
the meeting of the 5th of October,
at eight o'clock in the evening.
The President has a communication
of the utmost importance.
The Gun Club's notice
📜 The Gun Club: members are requested to attend the meeting of the 5th of October.
The crane over the Columbiad's mouth
look up at the crane
🏗️ The crane over the Columbiad's mouth.

🏗️ The crane over the Columbiad's mouth, and below it the well of the great gun, nine hundred feet straight down into the hill. ( Round the Moon begins here, once the Moon book you are in has been walked to its end.)
go to the telegraph
📡 The key and the sounder, and the wire to Tampa Town: news from the whole world comes in here, and goes out.
walk through the camp
⛺ Sheds of planks in rows, the men's cots, the canteen, the forge; a town built in a week for fifteen hundred workmen, on the hill where there was nothing.
The railway platform
wait for the train
🚂 The Gun Club's railway runs from here to Tampa Town, fifteen miles: rails, iron, coal, food and men come up it every day.
look at the furnaces
🔥 Twelve hundred reverberatory furnaces round the hill, each its own chimney, each fed with coal and iron, all to be lit together on the day of the casting.
the Observatory of Cambridge
Back in Baltimore, on the Gun Club's front.
🔭 The Observatory of Cambridge, Massachusetts. A white dome among the elms of the college, its shutter open on the night; inside, the great refractor.
The great refractor
look through the great refractor

🔭 The Moon, through the great refractor The Moon fills the eyepiece: grey seas and white mountains, the long black shadows of the craters along the line where night meets day. Two hundred and forty thousand miles away, and you can count the peaks.
THE MOON'S PATH · 1st DECEMBER
The Director's desk
✉️ Letters from every observatory in Europe; a fair copy, nearly finished, addressed To the President of the Gun Club at Baltimore.
study the star charts
🗺️ The Moon's path among the stars for the coming year, worked out to the second, and one night ringed in ink: the 1st of December.
The observatory gate
go home to Baltimore
Tampa Town, Florida
North by the steamer to Baltimore (the Gun Club's front, on the quay).

🌴 Tampa Town, Florida, 1866. A little town of wooden houses on Tampa Bay, grown in a year to a city: the quay full of steamers, the hotels full, the streets full of people come to see the Gun Club's great shot.
The Atlanta, at the quay
look at the Atlanta
🚢 The Atlanta, a steamer from Liverpool: smoke still coming from her funnel, her passengers' boxes piled on the quay, the whole of Tampa crowded to see her.
The quay of Tampa Town
walk along the quay
⚓ Tampa Bay: the steamers in from Mobile and New Orleans and New York, the barges for Stone's Hill, the bales, the barrels, the crowds.
The Franklin Hotel
go up to the rooms
🏨 The Franklin Hotel: every room taken since the Gun Club came, the veranda full of reporters, and a crowd in the street day and night under Barbicane's windows.
The telegraph office
go to the telegraph office
📡 The telegraph office: the clerks at their keys, the wire to the whole Union and, by the cable from Valentia, to Europe.
The platform on the meeting-field
go up to the platform
🎤 The platform outside the town, its flags snapping: the whole crowd of Tampa, and half of Florida, packed round it as far as you can see.
The great mortar of Pensacola
look at the mortar
💥 A huge mortar, brought from the arsenal at Pensacola, to try the shock of a shell on living creatures before any man goes.
The road to Stone's Hill
ride to Stone's Hill
🐎 Fifteen miles inland, through the pine woods and the swamps, up to Stone's Hill .
the wood of Skersnaw
🌳 The wood of Skersnaw , a mile and a half from Tampa: live oaks and magnolias, olives, tulip-trees, catalpas, the grey moss hanging; and somewhere in it, two men with rifles looking for each other.
drink from the stream
💧 Cold, clear water, running over sand under the trees. Somewhere a mocking-bird; nothing else.
The gigantic catalpa
look up into the catalpa
🌳 A great catalpa, twenty feet off the path, its leaves like hearts; and between two of its low branches, something caught and struggling.
look closer at the web
🐦 Gently, with Nicholl: the threads part, and the little bird is off into the trees.
🕸️ An empty web, torn, and a cross spider.
🕸️ A little bird, a fly-catcher, tangled in a spider's web; and a fat spider coming for it down the threads.
The way out of the wood
walk back to Tampa Town
The edge of the wood
look into the wood
🌲 Tall trees and grey moss, and no sound but the birds. Somewhere in there, Barbicane; somewhere else, Nicholl.
the bottom of the Columbiad
Up the nine hundred feet, and out on Stone's Hill.
🕳️ The bottom of the Columbiad , nine hundred feet under Stone's Hill: a polished iron well, nine feet across, lit by electric light; a table laid for the Gun Club.
sit down at the banquet
🍽️ Dinner nine hundred feet down: the toasts follow one another, the iron walls ring with hurrahs, and somebody has brought a cannon-ball for a centrepiece.
go up in the basket
The iron wall of the bore
🔩 Cold iron, polished like glass, nine hundred feet of it straight up to a little disc of blue sky.
Out of the projectile, onto Stone's Hill.
🌖 The projectile. Nine feet across inside, its walls padded with leather over steel springs; four thick glass scuttles; gas for light and heat; provisions for a year; two dogs; three men.
look out of the scuttle
The other side scuttle
look down through the floor
🎇 Barbicane touches the match to the fuses through the floor: the rockets in the base roar together, and the whole projectile shudders and turns.
The oxygen apparatus
look at the oxygen apparatus
🫧 You turn the tap down. The hiss dies; the gas-flame shrinks back to its proper yellow; one by one, everyone sits down, rather ashamed.
🫧 Reiset and Regnault's apparatus: it gives out fresh air for breathing, and takes up the breathed air. One tap, and the hand on it must be careful.
look at the gas lamp
💡 The gas-burner under the cone: light, and the heat that keeps the cold of space outside.
read Barbicane's notebook
📓 Columns of figures in a small exact hand: times, distances, speeds; and, underlined twice, 10.46.40, December 1.
look at the instruments
🌡️ Thermometers, a barometer, the telescopes, a chronometer set to the second, maps of the Moon by Beer and Mädler.
look in the chests
🥫 Meat and vegetables pressed hard and dry, enough for a year; brandy; water for two months; tea from the Emperor of Russia.
🐕 Diana and Satellite, Michel's dogs, curled up together on their blanket.
climb out of the projectile
🪟 The shutter rolls back from the glass.
🛡️ The shutter is down over the glass: nothing to see but riveted metal.
🔒 The hatch is screwed down tight, and outside it there is nothing at all: no air, and a cold no man could bear.
Long's Peak, Colorado
Down from the mountains, and home to Baltimore.
🏔️ Long's Peak, in the Rocky Mountains, 14,000 feet up. Snow, rock, thin cold air; and the greatest telescope in the world, its tube 280 feet long, its mirror sixteen feet across, aimed at the Moon.
The observers' hut
🛖 The observers' hut: a stove, a table of logbooks, the wire to Cambridge and to Baltimore, and hot coffee for men who watch all night.
The great telescope
look up at the telescope
🔭 A tube 280 feet long, laid up the mountain on its iron frame, its sixteen-foot mirror at the foot: through it the Moon comes to within five miles.
The eyepiece gallery
climb up to the eyepiece
🔭 The eyepiece gallery , high on the tube's mouth. Below, the whole of the Rockies under snow.
look through the great telescope
go down the mountain
A bright point against the Moon's black limb, moving: the projectile, going round her. A new star.
Cloud. Thick, grey, unbroken cloud, night after night.
The Moon, so near you could count the stones on her: the craters, the long shadows, the seas of grey, and no sign of any living thing.
🔭 Through the great telescope
the U.S.S. Susquehanna
Home by rail to Baltimore.
⚓ The U.S.S. Susquehanna , a steam frigate of the United States Navy, sounding the bed of the Pacific two hundred miles off the coast for the telegraph cable to be laid.
The sounding machine
watch the sounding line
🧵 The wire paying out from the drum, fathom after fathom, down into the dark: 3,000 fathoms, and the lead not yet at the bottom.
go up to the bridge
🧭 Captain Blomsberry's bridge: the chart of the Pacific, the course two hundred miles off the coast, latitude 27° 7' north.
☄️ A ball of fire, falling, growing, roaring, straight down into the sea a few hundred yards away: a column of steam and spray, and the ship heeling.
🌊 The Pacific, empty to the horizon. Boats out, grapples down, all day long.
🌊 Something bobbing on the swell, bright as silver in the sun: the projectile, afloat!
🌊 The Pacific, long and blue and calm, and the stars coming out.
The projectile, afloat
hail the projectile
🌊 Nothing there but the sea.
🌖 Bright metal on the swell; and from inside, faintly, through the scuttle... laughter? Dominoes?
look at the cutter
🚣 The Susquehanna's eight-oared cutter, ready to be lowered.
A sailor of the Susquehanna
Three thousand fathoms, and still no bottom!
Major Elphinston, sir. Let us take things in order.
General Morgan. Cast iron, or bronze? That is the question.
Peace! It's ruin, sir. Ruin.
Baltimore, after the War of the Rebellion
The Gun Club has its great hall on Union Square. Walk up the hall to the President's chair.
Tom Hunter is whittling the arms of his chair. Ask him how the members are.
Ridiculous!" replied Tom Hunter, whittling with his bowie-knife the arms of his easy chair; "but if that be the case there, all that is left for us is to plant tobacco and distill whale-oil.
The war is over, and a gunner with nothing to fire is a sad thing.
▶ 'And the others?'
Bilsby has an idea of his own about where the next war might be. Hear it.
What are you dreaming of?" screamed Bilsby; "work at gunnery for the benefit of foreigners?
Bah!" growled Bilsby between the four teeth which the war had left him; "that will never do!
🦾 What the war left them
The members of the Gun Club are proud of their wounds. Which of these is J. T. Maston's?
An iron hook for a hand, and a plate of gutta-percha over the top of his skull
Those are Tom Hunter's.
Maston, scratching with his steel hook his gutta-percha cranium.
J. T. Maston has a proposal of his own. Go to him at the table.
Well, then," replied J. T. Maston, "why should not England in her turn belong to the Americans?
The others shout him down: there is no war to be had, anywhere.
Look through the newspapers on the rack: perhaps there is a war somewhere.
A factory of fireworks
